blocks.text: A 29-year-old woman has never attended a screening invitation. She presents with bleeding after intercourse, and the cervix looks friable on speculum examination. The disease in front of you took perhaps 10 to 20 years to arrive, and for most of that time it was silent, detectable and treatable. This unit follows that timeline: the virus, the screening that intercepts it, and the cancer when interception fails.

blocks.markdown: **Anatomy first.** The cervix has an ectocervix covered by stratified squamous epithelium and an endocervical canal lined by columnar (glandular) epithelium. They meet at the **squamocolumnar junction (SCJ)**. At puberty and in pregnancy, columnar epithelium everts onto the ectocervix and is replaced by metaplastic squamous epithelium. The zone where this replacement occurs is the **transformation zone**. Immature metaplastic cells there are the most susceptible to persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which is why nearly all cervical neoplasia arises in the transformation zone and why screening samples and colposcopic examination focus on it.

blocks.title: HPV, CIN and carcinogenesis
blocks.text: High-risk HPV (hrHPV) types, chiefly 16 and 18 (together responsible for roughly 70% of cervical cancers), cause cancer when infection persists. The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 act by promoting degradation of p53 (E6) and inactivating the retinoblastoma protein Rb (E7), removing cell-cycle and apoptosis controls. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is the histological precancer, graded 1 to 3 by the proportion of epithelial thickness replaced by abnormal cells; CIN2 and CIN3 are 'high grade' and are treated.

blocks.markdown:
**Natural history.** Most HPV infections are acquired soon after sexual debut and are cleared by the immune system within about two years without any lesion. A minority persist. Persistence, not mere exposure, drives progression to high-grade CIN over years and to invasive cancer over a decade or more. Cofactors that favour persistence include **smoking, immunosuppression (HIV infection, transplant immunosuppression), long-term combined oral contraceptive use and high parity**. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type; adenocarcinoma arises from endocervical glands higher in the canal and is harder to detect by sampling the ectocervix.

**Vaccination (prevention before exposure).** HPV vaccines are made of virus-like particles, contain no viral DNA, and cannot cause infection. The UK programme uses a vaccine covering types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58, offered in school year 8 (age 12 to 13); the dose schedule has changed over time, so check the current schedule. Vaccination prevents new infection but does not treat an established infection or existing CIN, so **vaccinated women still need screening** (the vaccine does not cover every oncogenic type).

blocks.caption: Positive predictive value: TP = true positives (screen-positive women who have disease), FP = false positives. PPV falls as disease prevalence falls, even for a good test.

blocks.markdown:
**Screening.** Screening is aimed at a long, detectable, treatable preinvasive phase. In England, women aged 25 to 64 are invited (recall intervals depend on the HPV result and have been changing (3 to 5 years); follow the current NHS Cervical Screening Programme policy); the test is a **primary hrHPV test** on a liquid-based cytology sample. If hrHPV is negative, the woman returns to routine recall at the interval set by current policy. If hrHPV is positive, the same sample is examined by **cytology as a triage test**. Positive hrHPV with abnormal cytology leads to **colposcopy**. Positive hrHPV with normal cytology leads to repeat testing at 12 months, because many infections will clear. Screening is not diagnostic: histology from a biopsy is.

**Colposcopy** uses a binocular magnifying instrument to inspect the cervix after application of 3 to 5% acetic acid (abnormal epithelium with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio turns **acetowhite**) and sometimes Lugol's iodine (non-glycogenated abnormal epithelium stays unstained). Features of a higher-grade lesion include dense, rapidly appearing acetowhite change, sharp borders, **coarse punctation, coarse mosaic pattern and atypical vessels**. The colposcopist takes a directed biopsy, or performs **large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ)**, which both treats and provides histology for a high-grade lesion.

blocks.title: Triage of a positive screening result
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old woman has a routine primary hrHPV screening test. The result is hrHPV positive; reflex cytology is normal. Her follow-up test 12 months later is again hrHPV positive, with cytology showing high-grade dyskaryosis. Outline her pathway and the reasoning at each step.

steps.text: First result: hrHPV positive, cytology normal. Many HPV infections are transient and normal cytology means no visible cellular abnormality yet, so colposcopy now would over-investigate many women who will clear the virus. The pathway is repeat testing at 12 months.

Second result: hrHPV still positive after 12 months. Persistence has now been shown, the risk factor for progression. Cytology is now abnormal (high-grade dyskaryosis), which is the triage criterion for referral.

Action: refer for colposcopy. Directed biopsy or LLETZ is used to establish the histological grade. If CIN2 or CIN3 is confirmed, excision is offered and the woman is followed up with a test of cure using hrHPV testing.

blocks.answer: Repeat at 12 months after the first positive result with normal cytology, then colposcopy once persistence with abnormal cytology is demonstrated; histology guides treatment. (Check against current NHS cervical screening programme guidance.)

rows: Microinvasive; stromal invasion up to 5 mm depth
Cone excision or simple hysterectomy (with node assessment if lymphovascular space invasion or IA2)
Confined to cervix; IB1 = depth of invasion deeper than 5 mm with greatest dimension less than 2 cm; IB2 = greatest dimension 2 cm or more and less than 4 cm
Radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node assessment; fertility-sparing radical trachelectomy for selected small tumours
Confined to cervix, greatest dimension 4 cm or more (IB3); upper two-thirds of vagina involved (IIA)
Chemoradiation (IIA smaller tumours may be treated surgically)
Parametrial invasion not reaching the pelvic wall
Lower third vagina (A); pelvic wall or hydronephrosis (B); pelvic or para-aortic nodes (C)
Bladder or rectal mucosa (A); distant metastasis (B)
Chemoradiation (A selected); systemic therapy and palliation (B)
blocks.caption: Simplified staging and treatment principles. Stage is assigned using clinical examination, with imaging and pathology permitted in FIGO 2018.

blocks.markdown:
**Clinical presentation of invasive disease.** Postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, offensive vaginal discharge and pelvic pain; advanced disease causes back pain, leg swelling, haematuria, rectal symptoms and obstructive renal failure from ureteric compression. The cervix may be friable, ulcerated or barrel-shaped. Diagnosis is histological (punch biopsy or excision); the extent of disease is assessed by examination (including under anaesthesia), MRI of the pelvis for local extent, and CT or PET-CT for nodes and distant disease.

**Treatment principle.** Early disease confined to the cervix is surgical because radical hysterectomy offers cure while preserving ovarian function in premenopausal women. Locally advanced disease is treated with **concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation followed by brachytherapy**, because the cisplatin sensitises tumour cells to radiation. Combining radical surgery with radiotherapy is avoided where possible because their toxicities add (lymphoedema, bladder and bowel dysfunction, vaginal stenosis). Treatment doses and regimens are set by gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary teams.

blocks.title: Staging and choosing treatment
blocks.prompt: A 41-year-old woman has a biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma. MRI shows a 2.6 cm tumour confined to the cervix with no parametrial extension, and no pelvic nodes enlarged. She has completed her family. Assign the FIGO 2018 stage and outline treatment.

steps.text: Is the tumour confined to the cervix? Yes, so the stage is I. There is no vaginal or parametrial extension, no pelvic wall involvement and no nodal disease, which excludes stages II to IV.

Sub-classify by size: IB1 is invasive carcinoma with depth of invasion deeper than 5 mm and greatest dimension less than 2 cm, IB2 is 2 cm or more and less than 4 cm, IB3 is 4 cm or more. At 2.6 cm the tumour is IB2.

Treatment: because the disease is early and local, surgery is appropriate: radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node assessment. Fertility-sparing surgery is not required as childbearing is complete. If nodes proved positive or parametria involved on histology, adjuvant chemoradiation would be considered.

blocks.answer: Stage IB2; treat surgically with radical hysterectomy and pelvic lymph node assessment, with adjuvant chemoradiation only if adverse pathological features are found.

items: Screening targets the preinvasive phase and prevents cancer by finding and treating CIN, not by diagnosing cancer.
Vaccination reduces infection with the vaccine types; screening is still required.
Colposcopy identifies the transformation zone, acetowhite epithelium and abnormal vessels, and takes a biopsy for histology.
Staging determines whether treatment is surgical (early, up to about IB2) or chemoradiation (locally advanced).
Late complications of pelvic treatment include lymphoedema, bladder and bowel dysfunction, premature ovarian failure after radiotherapy and vaginal stenosis.

blocks.title: Do not delay assessment of postcoital bleeding
blocks.text: A woman with postcoital bleeding needs a speculum examination of the cervix and referral if abnormality is seen, whatever her screening history. A recent normal screening result does not exclude cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma, because screening has a false negative rate.

points: Persistent hrHPV infection (especially types 16 and 18, acting through E6 and E7) causes CIN and cervical cancer, usually over many years in the transformation zone.
HPV vaccination is prophylactic and complements, but does not replace, screening.
Primary hrHPV testing with cytology triage, then colposcopy and biopsy or LLETZ, finds and treats high-grade CIN.
FIGO staging guides therapy: surgery for early disease, platinum-based chemoradiation with brachytherapy for locally advanced disease.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the mechanism by which high-risk HPV types drive cervical neoplasia?

options.text: E6 promotes degradation of p53 and E7 inactivates the retinoblastoma protein
E6 inactivates the retinoblastoma protein and E7 promotes degradation of p53
The virus integrates a viral kinase that directly activates BRCA1
The virus causes neoplasia by lysing columnar cells in the endocervical canal

questions.correctOptionText: E6 promotes degradation of p53 and E7 inactivates the retinoblastoma protein

distractorRationale.a: Correct: E6 targets p53 for degradation and E7 binds and inactivates Rb.
distractorRationale.b: The targets of E6 and E7 are reversed.
distractorRationale.c: HPV does not carry a kinase that activates BRCA1; BRCA1 is a hereditary tumour suppressor unrelated to HPV oncogenesis.
distractorRationale.d: Oncogenesis relies on persistence and loss of cell-cycle control, not lytic destruction of cells.

questions.explanation: The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 remove two major brakes on the cell cycle. E6 leads to degradation of p53 (loss of apoptosis and DNA repair arrest) and E7 inactivates Rb (release of E2F and unchecked S-phase entry), allowing genetic damage to accumulate in persistently infected transformation zone cells.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl's mother asks whether HPV vaccination means her daughter will never need cervical screening. Which is the most accurate reply?

options.text: Screening will still be needed because the vaccine does not cover every oncogenic type and was designed to prevent infection, not treat it
Screening will not be needed because the vaccine contains live virus that gives lifelong immunity to all HPV types
Screening will not be needed provided she receives the vaccine after she becomes sexually active
Screening will be needed only if she develops postcoital bleeding

questions.correctOptionText: Screening will still be needed because the vaccine does not cover every oncogenic type and was designed to prevent infection, not treat it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the vaccine is prophylactic and covers selected types only.
distractorRationale.b: The vaccine uses virus-like particles with no viral DNA, and does not cover all HPV types.
distractorRationale.c: Vaccination works best before exposure, so delay until after sexual activity reduces benefit; it still does not remove the need for screening.
distractorRationale.d: Screening is population-based and offered to asymptomatic women; bleeding is an indication for assessment rather than the trigger for screening.

questions.explanation: HPV vaccines prevent new infection with the types they contain but do not cover every high-risk type and do not clear established infection. Screening therefore remains part of lifelong prevention for vaccinated and unvaccinated women alike.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman's routine screening sample is hrHPV positive and reflex cytology reports no abnormality. According to the principles of primary HPV screening in the UK, what is the next step?

options.text: Repeat the HPV test at 12 months
Immediate LLETZ
Return to routine recall without further testing
Total hysterectomy

questions.correctOptionText: Repeat the HPV test at 12 months

distractorRationale.a: Correct: many infections will clear, so retest after a year (check current programme guidance).
distractorRationale.b: Excision treats histologically proven high-grade disease; no lesion has been shown yet.
distractorRationale.c: An hrHPV-positive result cannot be ignored because it identifies increased risk of persistence.
distractorRationale.d: Hysterectomy is not a treatment for a positive screening test with normal cytology.

questions.explanation: The aim of triage is to avoid colposcopy for women whose infection will clear while keeping those with persistent infection under surveillance. A repeat test at 12 months identifies persistence, which is the risk factor for progression.

questions.stem: At colposcopy after application of acetic acid, which finding most strongly suggests a high-grade or invasive lesion needing biopsy?

options.text: Dense acetowhite epithelium with coarse mosaic pattern and atypical vessels
Faint, translucent acetowhite change that fades within seconds
Columnar epithelium visible on the ectocervix with a regular, fine vascular pattern
A smooth, pink ectocervix that stains dark brown with Lugol's iodine

questions.correctOptionText: Dense acetowhite epithelium with coarse mosaic pattern and atypical vessels

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dense, persistent acetowhite change with coarse mosaic and atypical vessels indicates more severe neoplasia.
distractorRationale.b: Faint, transient acetowhite change is typical of low-grade change or immature metaplasia.
distractorRationale.c: Ectopy of columnar epithelium is a normal finding at the SCJ.
distractorRationale.d: Normal glycogenated squamous epithelium stains dark brown with iodine.

questions.explanation: Abnormal epithelium has a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, so it turns densely and persistently white with acetic acid, and angiogenesis produces coarse and atypical vessel patterns. These signs direct the biopsy to the area most likely to contain high-grade disease or invasion.

questions.stem: A pilot programme screens 20,000 women. The prevalence of CIN2 or worse is 1.5%. The test has sensitivity 80% and specificity 95%. Calculate the positive predictive value (as a percentage) of a positive screening result for CIN2 or worse.
questions.explanation: Diseased women: 20,000 x 0.015 = 300. True positives = 300 x 0.80 = 240. Disease-free women = 19,700; false positives = 19,700 x 0.05 = 985. PPV = 240 / (240 + 985) = 240 / 1225 = 19.6%. Even a good test has a modest PPV at low prevalence, which is why positive screens lead to colposcopy and histology rather than treatment.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a squamous cell carcinoma confined to the cervix measuring 5 cm on MRI, with no nodal or parametrial involvement. What is the FIGO 2018 stage?

options.text: IB3
IB1
IIB
IIIA

distractorRationale.a: Correct: confined to the cervix and 4 cm or more in greatest dimension is IB3.
distractorRationale.b: IB1 is a tumour of less than 2 cm (with invasion deeper than 5 mm), so it is too small.
distractorRationale.c: IIB requires parametrial invasion, which is absent.
distractorRationale.d: IIIA requires involvement of the lower third of the vagina.

questions.explanation: Disease limited to the cervix is stage I, subdivided by size. Tumours 4 cm or more in greatest dimension (but confined to the cervix) are IB3, and these are usually treated with chemoradiation rather than surgery because the risk of needing adjuvant radiotherapy after surgery is high.

questions.stem: True or false: a cervical carcinoma with ureteric obstruction causing hydronephrosis is stage IIIB, even if the tumour on examination appears to be confined to the cervix.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In FIGO staging, hydronephrosis or a non-functioning kidney due to tumour causes at least stage IIIB, unless it has another known cause. Ureteric obstruction implies extension to the pelvic sidewall region regardless of how limited the lesion appears on examination.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is found to have FIGO stage IIB cervical cancer (parametrial invasion, pelvic wall not reached). Explain the principles of her treatment, why surgery is not the primary treatment, and two late complications of the therapy.
markingGuide: Primary treatment is concurrent platinum-based (cisplatin) chemotherapy with external beam pelvic radiotherapy
Followed by brachytherapy to deliver a high dose to the cervix and parametria
Cisplatin acts as a radiosensitiser, improving local control and survival compared with radiotherapy alone
Surgery not primary because parametrial invasion makes clear surgical margins unlikely and the woman would probably need adjuvant radiotherapy, combining toxicities
Management by gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team, with staging imaging such as MRI and CT or PET-CT
Late complications: any two of vaginal stenosis, lymphoedema, bladder or bowel dysfunction, premature ovarian failure, fistula
Mention that regimens and doses follow current guidelines
questions.explanation: Locally advanced disease with parametrial involvement is treated by chemoradiation followed by brachytherapy because radical hysterectomy cannot reliably clear the parametria and would commonly need adjuvant radiation. The cumulative pelvic radiation produces late effects, which must be discussed with the woman before treatment.

questions.stem: Explain why cervical cancer is a good candidate for a screening programme, and why primary HPV testing is used with cytology triage rather than cytology alone.
markingGuide: Important health problem with a known natural history: persistent hrHPV leading to CIN then invasive cancer
Long, detectable preinvasive phase of years, allowing time for detection
Acceptable and safe test, accessible transformation zone sampling
Effective treatment for precancer (LLETZ) that prevents cancer
HPV testing is more sensitive than cytology for CIN2 or worse and gives longer reassurance when negative, allowing longer recall intervals
Cytology as triage improves specificity because many HPV infections clear, reducing unnecessary colposcopy
Acknowledge limitations: false negatives, overtreatment and anxiety, and that screening does not replace vaccination
questions.explanation: Screening works because cervical cancer is preceded by a long, detectable and treatable precancer. Primary HPV testing is more sensitive than cytology alone, but most positive results are transient infections, so cytology triage keeps specificity acceptable and avoids needless colposcopy.

questions.stem: Which woman is at highest risk of persistent hrHPV infection and rapid progression to high-grade cervical neoplasia?

options.text: A 30-year-old woman with HIV infection who smokes 15 cigarettes a day
A 30-year-old nulliparous woman who uses a copper intrauterine device
A 30-year-old woman who has been vaccinated at age 12 and does not smoke
A 30-year-old woman who uses barrier contraception consistently

questions.correctOptionText: A 30-year-old woman with HIV infection who smokes 15 cigarettes a day

distractorRationale.a: Correct: immunosuppression and smoking both favour viral persistence.
distractorRationale.b: A copper IUD is not a risk factor for HPV persistence.
distractorRationale.c: Vaccination before exposure and non-smoking lower risk.
distractorRationale.d: Consistent condom use reduces, rather than increases, HPV transmission risk.

questions.explanation: Immune surveillance clears most HPV infections, so impaired cell-mediated immunity in HIV permits persistence. Smoking adds carcinogens concentrated in cervical mucus and reduces local immunity, further raising the risk of progression.
